title: Critical Connections in a Network
description: Brute force to optimized: removing each edge and checking connectivity from scratch versus a single DFS with discovery times and low-link values.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given n servers connected by undirected connections, forming a network, return all critical connections: edges (bridges) whose removal would disconnect part of the network from the rest.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Find edges whose removal disconnects the graph\"","The classic bridge-finding algorithm (Tarjan's), using DFS discovery times and low-link values"]]}

blocks.text: An edge (u, v), where v is discovered as a DFS child of u, is a bridge exactly when v's subtree has NO way to reach back to u or any of u's ancestors through some OTHER path (a "back edge"). Tracking, for every node, its DFS discovery time (disc) and the EARLIEST discovery time reachable from its subtree via back edges (low), an edge is a bridge precisely when the child's low value is STRICTLY GREATER than the parent's discovery time, meaning the child's subtree is entirely cut off from the rest of the graph if this one edge is removed.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Single Rope Bridges Connecting Otherwise Separate Mountain Villages
blocks.text: Picture a network of mountain villages connected by paths, some of which are simple single rope bridges. A rope bridge is critical exactly when its village on the far side has absolutely NO other path back to the near side, meaning cutting that one rope bridge would truly isolate that village and everything beyond it.

blocks.caption: An edge is a bridge if the child subtree cannot reach back to or above the parent via any other path

blocks.text: Result: [[1,3]] (nodes 0,1,2 form a triangle with two paths between any pair, so no edge among them is critical; but the single edge to node 3 is the only way to reach it).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Perform a DFS, assigning every node a discovery time (disc), the order it was first visited.

Observation 2: Also track a low-link value (low) for every node: the EARLIEST discovery time reachable from that node's subtree, including via "back edges" to already-visited ancestors (not just tree edges).

Observation 3: For a tree edge from parent u to child v, after fully exploring v's subtree, update low[u] to be at most low[v] (u can reach whatever v's subtree can reach).

Observation 4: If low[v] is STRICTLY GREATER than disc[u], it means v's subtree has NO back edge reaching u or higher, so the edge (u, v) is the ONLY connection for that entire subtree, making it a bridge.

Observation 5: For a "back edge" encountered (to an already-visited node that is not the immediate parent), update low[u] using the ANCESTOR's discovery time directly (not its low value), since a back edge reaches exactly that ancestor's position in the DFS tree.
This leads to a single DFS computing discovery times and low-link values, identifying every bridge via the low[child] greater than disc[parent] condition.
For each edge, temporarily remove it and run a full connectivity check (DFS/BFS or Union-Find) from scratch to see if the graph becomes disconnected.
Why the code is written this way

items: Removing each edge and checking connectivity directly implements the definition of a bridge.
This repeats a full graph traversal for EVERY edge, costing O(edges times (nodes plus edges)) overall; a single combined DFS with low-link values identifies every bridge in one pass.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(edges times (nodes plus edges)).
Space: O(nodes plus edges) per check.
Limitation: a single DFS computing discovery times and low-link values identifies every bridge simultaneously, without needing a separate traversal per edge.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build an adjacency list. Maintain disc and low arrays, both initially -1 (unvisited), and a running timer. Define dfs(u, parent): assign disc[u] = low[u] = the current timer value, incrementing it. For each neighbor v of u (skipping the immediate parent, to avoid trivially treating the tree edge back to the parent as a back edge): if v is unvisited, recursively dfs(v, u), then update low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]), and if low[v] is greater than disc[u], record (u, v) as a bridge. If v is already visited (a back edge), update low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v]) directly.
Use a single DFS computing discovery times and low-link values, identifying bridges via the low[child] greater than disc[parent] condition.

blocks.text: The low-link value of a node correctly represents the earliest (smallest discovery time) node reachable from its entire subtree, whether directly or via any back edge; if a child's low value is STRICTLY GREATER than its parent's own discovery time, it proves the child's subtree has absolutely no alternate way back to the parent or anything above it, meaning the single tree edge connecting them is the ONLY path, making it a bridge; skipping the trivial edge directly back to the immediate parent avoids incorrectly treating that necessary tree edge itself as a false "back edge".

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(nodes plus edges), a single DFS.
Space: O(nodes plus edges) for the adjacency list and disc/low arrays.

blocks.text: Critical Connections in a Network is the classic bridge-finding problem (Tarjan's algorithm), a cornerstone technique in network reliability analysis.

items: Forgetting to skip the trivial edge directly back to the immediate parent, incorrectly treating it as a back edge and corrupting the low-link computation.
Updating low[u] using low[v] instead of disc[v] for an actual back edge (the two updates use different source values and are easy to confuse).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "find edges whose removal disconnects the graph", think: Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm using DFS discovery times and low-link values.

items: How would you adapt this same technique to find ARTICULATION POINTS (critical nodes) instead of critical edges?
Articulation points and strongly connected components (Tarjan's SCC algorithm), both closely related low-link-value techniques.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The per-edge removal brute force costs O(edges times (nodes plus edges)); the single-DFS approach costs O(nodes plus edges), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm, using DFS discovery times and low-link values.
Core Idea: an edge is a bridge exactly when the child's low-link value is strictly greater than the parent's discovery time.
Time: O(edges times (nodes plus edges)) for the brute force, O(nodes plus edges) for the single-DFS approach.
Most Important Observation: skip the trivial edge back to the immediate parent when checking for back edges.
Interview Difficulty: a hard, classic graph theory algorithm problem.
One line memory trick: low[child] greater than disc[parent] means a bridge.
